descriptors.R: nominee of the party that won control of the House in a landslide in the 1894 elections
descriptors.D: nominee of the party of the administration in office since 1893, chosen on a free-silver platform that breaks with the administration's gold policy, and also endorsed by the farmer-labor third party

compile_desc.R: the party that won control of the House in the 1894 elections
compile_desc.D: the party of the administration in office since 1893

others_line: Other candidates on some ballots, including a gold-standard breakaway ticket, a Prohibition nominee and a Socialist Labor nominee (answer "other").
never_name: McKinley, Bryan, Hobart, Sewall, Watson, Palmer, Buckner, Hanna, Altgeld, Reed or Cleveland

slice_sources.men: 1890 and 1900 censuses interpolated to November 1896; men 21+ outside the eleven Southern states (including declarant aliens where they could vote); turnout and choice from the backbone, calibrated to certified 1896 returns.
slice_sources.women: 1890 and 1900 censuses interpolated to November 1896; women 21+ outside the South; women could vote for president only in Wyoming, Colorado (1893) and Utah (statehood, January 1896); Idaho's amendment was adopted at this same election, so Idaho women first voted in 1898.
slice_sources.south-white: 1890 and 1900 censuses interpolated to November 1896; white adults in the eleven former Confederate states (includes a small number of American Indian and Asian adults); calibrated to certified 1896 returns.
slice_sources.black-south: 1890 and 1900 censuses interpolated to November 1896; Black adults in the eleven former Confederate states; disfranchisement was intensifying (Mississippi 1890, South Carolina 1895, poll taxes and registration laws elsewhere); the shortfall against white turnout is counted as exclusion.
slice_sources.immigrants: 1890 and 1900 censuses interpolated to November 1896; foreign-born white adults who were aliens or had only declared their intent (first papers); declarant aliens could vote in several Midwestern and Western states (fewer each decade as states repealed it), so part of this slice could vote.

masks: the House majority party's campaign manager
